chunks.heading: What is a function?
chunks.body: A function is a rule that takes an input number and gives back exactly one output number. We call the input x and the output y.
chunks.checkText: A function gives, for each input, ...

chunks.heading: Writing f(x) instead of y
chunks.body: f(x) is another way to write a [[mathadv-function-idea|function]]'s output for a given input x. If f(x) = x + 5, then f(3) means put x = 3 in, giving f(3) = 8.
chunks.checkText: If f(x) = x + 5, what is f(0)?

chunks.heading: The domain: which x-values are allowed
chunks.body: The domain of a [[mathadv-function-idea|function]] is the set of all x-values it's allowed to use as inputs.
chunks.checkText: The domain of a function is the set of all its possible...

chunks.heading: The range: which y-values come out
chunks.body: The [[mathadv-domain|domain]] is the inputs allowed; the range is the set of y-values a function actually produces as outputs.
chunks.checkText: The range of a function is its set of possible...

chunks.heading: The natural domain: values that just don't work
chunks.body: If no domain is stated, we use every x-value that makes the rule work — this is called the natural domain. We can't divide by zero, and we can't take the square root of a negative number.
chunks.checkText: y = 1/x has no natural domain value at x = ...

chunks.heading: A relation: any pairing of x and y
chunks.body: A relation is any set of paired x and y values, shown as points on a graph. It doesn't need any special rule about how many y-values go with each x.
chunks.checkText: A relation is...

chunks.heading: Every function is a relation, but not the reverse
chunks.body: A [[mathadv-function-idea|function]] is a special [[mathadv-relation-idea|relation]] where each x-value is paired with only one y-value. A relation can pair one x-value with several y-values.
chunks.checkText: What makes a relation a function?

Each y has only one x
It must be a straight line

chunks.heading: Testing for a function: the vertical line test
chunks.body: Draw a vertical line through a graph. If it ever crosses the graph more than once, the graph is not a [[mathadv-function-idea|function]].
chunks.checkText: A graph fails the vertical line test when a vertical line...

checkOptions.text: Crosses the graph more than once

chunks.heading: Testing for one-to-one: the horizontal line test
chunks.body: Draw a horizontal line through a graph. If it ever crosses the graph more than once, some y-value is matched to more than one x-value.
chunks.checkText: The horizontal line test checks whether...

checkOptions.text: One y-value matches more than one x-value
The graph passes through the origin

chunks.heading: One-to-one: every input and output is unique
chunks.body: A function passes both the [[mathadv-vertical-line-test|vertical]] and [[mathadv-horizontal-line-test|horizontal]] line tests. Each x gives exactly one y, and each y comes from exactly one x.
chunks.checkText: A one-to-one function passes...

checkOptions.text: Both the vertical and horizontal line tests

chunks.heading: Many-to-one: several inputs share an output
chunks.body: A [[mathadv-function-idea|function]] like y = x^2 is many-to-one: it passes the [[mathadv-vertical-line-test|vertical line test]] but fails the [[mathadv-horizontal-line-test|horizontal line test]], because different x-values can give the same y.
chunks.checkText: Which type of function is y = x^2?

chunks.heading: One-to-many: a relation, not a function
chunks.body: A relation like y^2 = x is one-to-many: it fails the [[mathadv-vertical-line-test|vertical line test]] but passes the [[mathadv-horizontal-line-test|horizontal line test]]. One x-value can give more than one y-value.
chunks.checkText: A one-to-many relation fails which test?

chunks.heading: Many-to-many: fails both tests
chunks.body: A relation like a circle is many-to-many: it fails both the [[mathadv-vertical-line-test|vertical]] and [[mathadv-horizontal-line-test|horizontal]] line tests.

chunks.heading: What is a quadratic function?
chunks.body: A quadratic function has the form f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, where a is not zero. Its graph is always a curve called a parabola.
chunks.checkText: In a quadratic function, which coefficient can never be zero?

chunks.heading: Which way does the parabola open?
chunks.body: In a [[mathadv-quadratic-function|quadratic function]] y = ax^2 + bx + c, a positive value of a makes the parabola open upward. A negative value of a makes it open downward.
chunks.checkText: If a is negative, the parabola opens...

chunks.heading: Zeroes: where the parabola crosses the x-axis
chunks.body: The zeroes of a [[mathadv-quadratic-function|quadratic function]] are its x-intercepts, found by setting y = 0. A parabola can have two zeroes, one zero, or none at all.
chunks.checkText: The zeroes of a function are found by setting...

chunks.heading: Finding zeroes by factoring
chunks.body: If a [[mathadv-quadratic-function|quadratic]] factors as y = (x − p)(x − q), then setting y = 0 gives zeroes x = p and x = q.
chunks.checkText: If y = (x − 2)(x + 5), the zeroes are...

chunks.heading: The axis of symmetry sits between the zeroes
chunks.body: A parabola's axis of symmetry is the vertical line exactly midway between its [[mathadv-quadratic-zeroes|zeroes]]. Its x-value is the average of the two zeroes.
chunks.checkText: If the zeroes are x = 1 and x = 5, the axis of symmetry is...

chunks.heading: Finding the vertex
chunks.body: The vertex is the parabola's turning point. Substitute the [[mathadv-axis-of-symmetry|axis of symmetry]]'s x-value back into the quadratic to find the vertex's y-value.
chunks.checkText: To find the vertex's y-value, you substitute the axis of symmetry into...

chunks.heading: Completing the square: rewriting a quadratic
chunks.body: Completing the square rewrites a [[mathadv-quadratic-function|quadratic]] as a(x − h)^2 + k, a perfect square plus a constant. This form makes the vertex easy to read off.
chunks.checkText: Completing the square rewrites a quadratic as...

checkOptions.text: A perfect square plus a constant

chunks.heading: How to complete the square
chunks.body: For x^2 + bx, halve b, then square the result, then add and subtract that number. This turns x^2 + bx into a [[mathadv-completing-square-idea|perfect square]] plus a constant.
chunks.checkText: To complete the square on x^2 + 6x, you halve 6 to get 3, then...

chunks.heading: Reading the vertex straight off
chunks.body: Once a quadratic is written as y = a(x − h)^2 + k using [[mathadv-completing-square-steps|completing the square]], the vertex is simply (h, k) — no extra working needed.

chunks.heading: The quadratic formula finds the zeroes
chunks.body: For y = ax^2 + bx + c, the [[mathadv-quadratic-zeroes|zeroes]] are x = (−b + sqrt(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a) and x = (−b − sqrt(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a).

chunks.heading: The discriminant: what's under the square root
chunks.body: The discriminant is Δ = b^2 − 4ac, the part of the [[mathadv-quadratic-formula|quadratic formula]] under the square root sign.

chunks.heading: What the discriminant tells you
chunks.body: If [[mathadv-discriminant|Δ]] is positive, the parabola has two zeroes. If Δ is zero, it has one zero. If Δ is negative, it has no zeroes.

chunks.heading: The cube of x: an S-shaped curve
chunks.body: The graph of y = x^3 passes through the origin and flattens out there. It's negative for negative x and positive for positive x.

chunks.heading: What is a polynomial?
chunks.body: A polynomial is an expression built from whole-number powers of x added together, like x^3 − 2x + 5. Its degree is the highest power of x used.

chunks.heading: Sketching from factors
chunks.body: If a [[mathadv-polynomial-def|polynomial]] is fully factored, like y = (x + 1)(x − 2)(x − 4), its zeroes are the values that make each factor zero.

chunks.heading: A repeated zero: touch, don't cross
chunks.body: If a factor like (x − a) is squared in a [[mathadv-polynomial-def|polynomial]], the curve touches the x-axis at x = a but doesn't cross it there.

chunks.heading: The square root function
chunks.body: y = sqrt(x) only gives the positive square root, so its graph only exists for x ≥ 0 and only ever gives y ≥ 0.
chunks.checkText: The graph of y = sqrt(x) exists for which x-values?

chunks.heading: The equation of a circle
chunks.body: A circle centred at the origin with radius a has equation x^2 + y^2 = a^2. This comes straight from Pythagoras' theorem.

chunks.heading: Splitting a circle into two functions
chunks.body: A [[mathadv-circle-equation|circle]]'s equation fails the vertical line test, so it isn't a function. But y = sqrt(a^2 − x^2) is the upper semicircle alone, which is a function.

chunks.heading: What is an asymptote?
chunks.body: An asymptote is a line that a graph gets closer and closer to, but never actually touches.
chunks.checkText: A graph and its asymptote...

chunks.heading: Exponential functions
chunks.body: An exponential function like y = a^x always has y-intercept 1, and the x-axis (y = 0) as an [[mathadv-asymptote-idea|asymptote]].
chunks.checkText: The y-intercept of y = a^x is always...

chunks.heading: The hyperbola: y = 1/x
chunks.body: The graph of y = 1/x has two separate branches, with [[mathadv-asymptote-idea|asymptotes]] along both the x-axis and the y-axis.
chunks.checkText: The hyperbola y = 1/x has how many asymptotes?

chunks.heading: Direct variation: y grows with x
chunks.body: y varies directly with x if y = kx for some constant k. Its graph is a straight line through the origin.

checkOptions.text: A straight line through the origin

chunks.heading: Inverse variation: y shrinks as x grows
chunks.body: y varies inversely with x if y = k/x for some constant k. Its graph is a [[mathadv-hyperbola|hyperbola]].

chunks.heading: Shifting a graph left or right
chunks.body: To shift a graph h units to the right, replace x with (x − h) in its equation. Shifting left works the same way, using a negative h.

chunks.heading: Shifting a graph up or down
chunks.body: To shift a graph k units up, add k to the whole function: y = f(x) + k. Shifting down uses a negative k.

chunks.body: A [[mathadv-circle-equation|circle]] centred at (h, k) with radius r has equation (x − h)^2 + (y − k)^2 = r^2 — the circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2 shifted to a new centre.

chunks.heading: Reflecting in the y-axis
chunks.body: To reflect a graph in the y-axis, replace x with −x. For a function, this gives the new rule y = f(−x).

chunks.heading: Reflecting in the x-axis
chunks.body: To reflect a graph in the x-axis, replace y with −y. For a function, this gives the new rule y = −f(x).

chunks.heading: Rotating 180° about the origin
chunks.body: Doing a [[mathadv-reflect-x-axis|reflection in the x-axis]] and a [[mathadv-reflect-y-axis|reflection in the y-axis]] together is the same as rotating the graph 180° about the origin.

chunks.heading: Even functions: mirror images in the y-axis
chunks.body: A function is even if f(−x) = f(x) for every x. Its graph looks the same after [[mathadv-reflect-y-axis|reflecting in the y-axis]].
chunks.checkText: An even function's graph has symmetry in...

chunks.heading: Odd functions: symmetric through the origin
chunks.body: A function is odd if f(−x) = −f(x) for every x. Its graph looks the same after [[mathadv-rotate-180|rotating 180° about the origin]].
chunks.checkText: An odd function satisfies which rule?

chunks.heading: Absolute value: distance from zero
chunks.body: The absolute value |x| is the distance from x to zero on the number line, so it's never negative. For example, |-5| = 5 and |5| = 5.

chunks.heading: The V-shaped graph of y = |x|
chunks.body: The graph of y = [[mathadv-absolute-value-idea|absolute value]] |x| is a V-shape with its sharp point at the origin. It's made of two straight line pieces.

chunks.heading: Solving |ax + b| = k
chunks.body: To solve |ax + b| = k, there are two solutions if k is positive, one solution if k is zero, and no solutions if k is negative.

chunks.heading: Composite functions: functions inside functions
chunks.body: The composite g(f(x)) means first apply f to x, then apply g to that result. It combines two functions into one new rule.
chunks.checkText: In g(f(x)), which function is applied first?

chunks.heading: Order matters for composites
chunks.body: In general, [[mathadv-composite-function|g(f(x))]] and f(g(x)) are different functions — swapping the order usually changes the result.
chunks.checkText: If f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = x^2, is g(f(x)) the same as f(g(x)) in general?

chunks.heading: The domain of a composite function
chunks.body: For a to be in the domain of [[mathadv-composite-function|g(f(x))]], a must work in f(x) first, and then f(a) must work in g(x) too.
